extracted.intended_audience: general public, householders, caregivers, nurses and local health officials (early 20th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical public-health prescriptions for preventing, controlling, and treating tuberculosis, pneumonia, and typhoid fever—covering personal habits, home and sanitarium care, disinfection, food/rest/air regimens, and water/milk sanitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not spit in public or on floors
rubrics_metrics.description: DON'T SPIT on the sidewalks; it spreads disease, and it is against the law. DON'T SPIT on the floors of your rooms or hallways. DON'T SPIT on the floors of your shop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spitting is filthy and spreads tuberculosis; injunctions against spitting apply in streets and public buildings as well as the individual home. Provide spittoons or gutters for expectoration rather than allowing indiscriminate spitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and maintain spittoons properly
rubrics_metrics.description: WHEN YOU SPIT, spit in the gutters or into a spittoon. Have your own spittoons half full of water, and clean them out at least once a day with hot water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep spittoons half full of water to prevent aerosolization and dry crusting; clean daily with hot water to disinfect and remove infectious material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover mouth when coughing
rubrics_metrics.description: DON'T cough without holding your handkerchief or your hand over your mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coughing dislodges small particles of sputum that may spread infection; consumptives must always hold a handkerchief over the mouth to prevent distributing infectious particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure continual fresh air in living/working/sleeping rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: DON'T live in rooms where there is no fresh air. DON'T work in rooms where there is no fresh air. DON'T sleep in rooms where there is no fresh air. Keep at least one window open in your bedroom day and night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fresh air reduces viability/transmission of respiratory germs and strengthens the individual; sleeping/working in ventilated spaces is emphasized as essential prevention and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wash hands before eating
rubrics_metrics.description: DON'T eat with soiled hands; wash them first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hand cleanliness prevents transmission of many infectious agents (noted specifically for preventing spread of tuberculosis/pneumonia/typhoid in the household).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not neglect colds or persistent coughs; seek early diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: DON'T NEGLECT A COLD or a cough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early recognition and treatment is critical—physicians may miss early tuberculosis by treating as catarrh or bronchitis; family history, temperature records, listlessness, and weight loss are important early indicators prompting expert examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinfect sputum and expectoration immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: When he spits, he must appreciate and act on the fact that the sputum is alive with consumptive germs... The patient must keep in mind continually that this sputum is poison ... he must see that every particle of it is disinfected or destroyed by one of the methods already indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectorate into a vessel filled with carbolic acid solution or into water to be afterwards boiled; use cloth or paper (e.g., Japanese napkin) that can be burned. Above all, do not expectorate indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumptive patients must use and disinfect their own eating utensils
rubrics_metrics.description: The eating utensils used by a consumptive patient must not in any way be allowed to infect other people. The consumptive must have his own dishes reserved exclusively for him, and they must be, after each meal, carefully disinfected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve exclusive dishes for the sick person and disinfect them after every meal to prevent fomite transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid direct contact (kissing) with consumptives
rubrics_metrics.description: With these precautions and with avoidance of such practices as kissing or otherwise directly infecting others, there is no reason why a consumptive patient should be ... in perfect safety to himself and to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid close personal contact that can transmit sputum or respiratory secretions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin treatment early for favorable prognosis
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief factor in the cure of consumption is the time at which the attempt at cure is started... If taken in time ... as large a proportion of consumptive patients may recover as of patients from typhoid fever or diphtheria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early detection and immediate adoption of treatment measures (sanitarium care or home regimen) markedly improve recovery rates; delayed diagnosis by ordinary physicians can miss the window for cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build up individual resistance: food, rest, and fresh air
rubrics_metrics.description: The three remedies, which are nature's own methods, are good food, fresh air, and rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three are essential and synergistic: thorough nourishment (eggs, milk emphasized), absolute rest (restricted activity), and continuous fresh air form the core of both prevention and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribe absolute rest and avoid exertion for tuberculosis patients
rubrics_metrics.description: All exercise taken by a tuberculous patient means the withdrawing of that much blood from the lungs ... one of the most striking features of sanitarium treatment is the absolute rest enjoined on the patients. Flat on their backs, day and night for months ... the effect of disobedience is plainly seen in the rise in temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict rest regimen—often reclined with head down and feet up—is required; even minor exertion can cause fever spikes and worsen disease; sanitarium routines or strict home adherence are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresh-air therapy: continuous outdoor exposure for consumptives
rubrics_metrics.description: The patient must spend twenty-four hours a day in the open. He must eat and sleep out of doors ... the side porch of a house may be very easily transformed into a room with a cot bed ... If no side porch exists ... windows of a room may be left open all the time, or the patient may lie on a bed, the head of which either extends through the window or is arranged to admit fresh air by a specially devised window tent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain outdoor exposure as much as possible regardless of season (wrap up to avoid cold) or create appropriate outdoor/ventilated sleeping accommodations; fresh-air exposure is portrayed as decisive in arresting the disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote public sanitation and education to reduce mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational campaigns have been vigorously prosecuted ... The time is not far distant when those states and municipalities which have not adopted a comprehensive plan for dealing with tuberculosis will be regarded as almost criminally negligent ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt comprehensive municipal/state plans for tuberculosis control—education, sanitation, ventilation, and institutional care produce marked population-level mortality decrease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pneumonia treatment: keep the sick room well ventilated and supply fresh air
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, a pneumonia patient is supplied with all the fresh air possible, the windows of the sick room, even in winter, being kept continually open ... children and babies suffering with pneumonia are at once taken there [to roof wards] ... nurses and physicians don fur coats ... the pneumonia germ, under these conditions, is worsted almost as if by magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to older practice of heated, moist atmospheres, pneumonia patients benefit from abundant fresh air even in winter; special wards/tents with open ventilation are effective despite patient discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent pneumonia by preserving bodily vigor: sleep, diet, exercise, bathing, ventilation
rubrics_metrics.description: The best remedy and the best prevention for pneumonia is a careful attention to the needs of the body ... Regular hours, sufficient sleep, and good food ... more fresh air, with better food, with ample bathing ... more outdoor life in the winter time, and more exercise ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain routine healthy habits and adequate ventilation to keep resistance high; this prevents pneumonia more effectively than avoiding exposure to cold alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pneumonia infection control: sterilize utensils and laundry; protect caregivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The eating utensils, food refuse, and soiled clothing may all be infectious and must be sterilized by boiling as soon as removed from the sick room. The nurse should be particularly careful not to infect herself. She should be careful to exercise enough self-control always to get daily exercise and fresh air and must, as a matter of self-protection, avoid overfatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boil potentially contaminated materials; caregivers must avoid overwork, maintain their own fresh air/exercise to reduce susceptibility, and follow disinfection procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid control: eliminate transmission by disinfecting fecal discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: Entirely to deprive the germs of life, therefore, it is necessary ... to act promptly and at once disinfect the fecal discharges from the patient rather than to wait ... There is probably no more important thing in stopping the spread of typhoid fever than to practice carefully disinfection in the sick room, using bichloride of mercury and chloride of lime, as already described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt, routine disinfection of feces and soiled materials in the sick-room with specified disinfectants is paramount to preventing spread to water, soil, or food.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boil suspect water and use heat/pasteurization to kill typhoid germs
rubrics_metrics.description: A high temperature kills typhoid fever germs ... 160 degrees Fahrenheit for ten minutes will kill any typhoid fever germs present. Boiling, of course ... will kill the germs, and it is for this reason that wherever a water is suspected of typhoid pollution, it should be boiled before being used for drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sterilize suspect drinking water by boiling; pasteurize milk (160°F for 10 minutes) to remove infection risk; heating is reliable where contamination is suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize main transmission routes and focus on water safety
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three main avenues used by the germ, namely, water, milk, and flies, and of these three, the first is by far the most important and includes probably 80 per cent of all the cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize protection of public water supplies (filtration, avoiding contamination) because waterborne spread accounts for the majority of typhoid cases; boil or avoid suspect sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct and protect wells to prevent typhoid contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Two points already mentioned are essential if well water is to be kept pure. One is to line the well with a water-tight masonry lining, and the other point is to have the cover of the well made with a thoroughly water-tight coating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use watertight masonry linings and sealed covers; avoid siting wells near privies; be aware of local geology (fissured rock, limestone) that can permit lateral contamination; sand/gravel soils are less risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid milk contamination by good handling and clean water
rubrics_metrics.description: Milk is responsible for perhaps 5 per cent of the cases of infection. ... milk frequently becomes infected because infected water has been added to it or because the cans have been washed in infected water, or because some persons in contact with a typhoid patient have had their hands infected and then handled the milk or the milk utensils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent milk-borne typhoid by ensuring milk is not diluted with contaminated water, milk cans and utensils are washed in safe water, and milk-handling personnel are uninfected and practice hand hygiene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand environmental survival of typhoid bacillus to guide measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Drying kills the typhoid bacillus in a few hours ... the direct rays of the sun will kill typhoid fever germs within a few hours ... in distilled water ... the germs will live about a month ... in water rich in organic matter ... the period may be extended two or three times ... In the ground, the life of the bacteria is longer ... they may live several months, if not a year or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of how heat, drying, sunlight, cold/ice, and organic content affect survival to inform sterilization, water-supply protection, timing of contamination risk, and decisions to boil or avoid particular sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act promptly on suspected water pollution: avoid or sterilize it
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral of these incidents is very plain, namely, that where any possibility of the infection of drinking water occurs, that water ought either to be avoided or else to be thoroughly sterilized before using.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pollution of a spring, well, or stream is suspected (e.g., nearby privies, recent cases upstream), either avoid using the water or boil/sterilize it; shutting off contaminated supplies and installing filtration stops epidemics.
